articles.title: Trying To Move Thanksgiving Has Not Gone Well, Historically Speaking
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Thanksgiving’s date is set by federal law as the fourth Thursday in November — but that law exists only because a president once tried to move the holiday himself. In 1939, at the urging of retailers who wanted a longer Christmas shopping season, he proclaimed Thanksgiving a week early. States revolted, the calendar descended into chaos, and the rescheduled holiday picked up what mocking nickname?

Hint: The president was Franklin D. Roosevelt, who did it three years running. The country split — nearly half the states kept the traditional date, and a few observed both — until Congress ended the mess by fixing Thanksgiving in law, choosing the fourth Thursday over the last.

See the answer on the next page.

The post Trying To Move Thanksgiving Has Not Gone Well, Historically Speaking appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: 3 More Questions For A Patent Litigator Turned Legal Recruiter (Part II)
articles.content:
Last time, I presented Part 1 of my written interview with a former patent litigator turned legal recruiter, Khurram Naik. That column presented his answer to the first of my three questions and focused on the lessons shared by his podcast guests that have relevance to his lateral candidates. What follows are Khurram’s answers to my remaining two questions. As usual, I have added some brief commentary to his answers below, but have otherwise presented his answers as he provided them.
Gaston Kroub: What’s the role of a legal podcast like yours?
Khurram Naik: Legal media focus on outcomes, like what a court decided in a particular matter. But there’s little insight into the process that led to those outcomes. Lawyers make concerted decisions over a period of time and develop the judgement to direct those outcomes. That’s what the podcast uncovers.
There is the problem of the vanilla middle. So many interviews with lawyers have rehearsed answers to softball questions. What I’ve found much more interesting are the bookends to the vanilla middle: 1) what are the real challenges and setbacks exceptional lawyers face, and 2) what are the smart calls they’ve made.
The first inquiry humanizes skilled lawyers so we can actually learn from them. The second inquiry sidesteps the “I’m humbled to announce, it was a team effort, etc.” reaction to discussing successes so we can actually learn what someone did that was skillful.
Take Rohit Nath’s interview. As we explored how he was early to the AI copyright disputes, he shared that he had read the Supreme Court’s Warhol Foundation opinion more than 100 times while he was thinking about how to litigate fair use. I find that amazing. No one tells you to read a Supreme Court decision 100 times. There’s no prize for doing it. It comes purely out of a relentless curiosity. But we can uniquely learn how exceptional lawyers operate from this podcast format.
GK: As much as I love this written interview format — and believe that it allows my interviewees to share insights that we can all learn from — I have to agree with Khurram that the long-form podcast format may be the optimal way to draw out the best in interviewees. And I also agree that giving his guests room to explore how they have overcome challenges and made great calls is a very worthwhile approach to take when interviewing lawyers at the top of their profession. It is important to remember that part of the beautiful brutality of high-end legal practice is the fact that we operate in a profession that both attracts exceptional intellectual talent and provides that talent with a canvas to express itself. In a meaningful way, Khurram’s podcast helps showcase that talent, while also giving us a peek into the process and curiosity that allows that intellectual firepower to burst forth. I especially like his mention of Rohit’s preparation process in his landmark AI wins for a number of reasons. First, because that was a highlight for me of that interview, containing as it did both inspiration and a hint of rebuke for those of us that aspire to excellence. Second, because I have had the good fortune of having Rohit be part of a team representing one of our patent-owning entities, and he is awesome on every level.
GK: Looking down the road, who else is on your wish list? What kinds of future guests are you hoping to bring on, and what’s the next big career challenge or legal market trend you’re interested in hearing from them on?”
KN: I’d love to interview more federal judges. I’ve interviewed two sitting district court judges, Judge Vince Chhabria and Judge Matthew Kennelly. I’m working on an interview with another district court judge now. Judges have to make a lot of decisions with limited information and resources, so they have differentiated insights on decision-making.
I’ve interviewed several lawyers who are litigating key disputes involving AI companies’ use of copyrighted materials — Louis Tompros, Sonal Mehta, Rohit Nath, and Paven Malhotra. These lawyers are on both sides of the v, so they represent a range of views. I’m fascinated how lawyers arrive early to a space, and the foundation they laid to get there, often inadvertently, by pursuing interesting and often small matters.
I’m interviewing more in-house lawyers. I’m interested in how they chose their path, which is desirable for many outside counsel but comes with much less direction. They’re making decisions under uncertainty. And they reveal how outside counsel do their most effective work.
GK: Khurram’s answer on interviewing more sitting trial judges will resonate with everyone who has been lucky enough to attend a Bench-Bar conference and appreciates how much you can learn from jurists as they speak in that type of sitting. To have a judge willing to go even more in-depth on a long-form podcast can only be even more informative. The need to learn from sitting judges is perhaps even more acute for IP litigators, whose practices can span multiple districts and a variety of judges with different levels of interest in — or tolerance of — the complexities of IP litigation. Likewise, hearing from practitioners on the different sides of a hot-button IP legal issue can also be fascinating, so I hope that Khurram can continue to attract the pioneers to sit down with him.
Lastly, the in-house perspective is perhaps the one I have been least able to share on these pages over the years, which is a regrettable circumstance as there is much to learn from the stories of in-house folks. In fact, I always find discussions with in-house folks very interesting, especially in a podcast format, since the stories around how they have arrived at their current roles are usually more interesting than those of who have simply hopped from clerkship to law firm A to law firm B. (For a good recent example, this discussion with Joseph Salama of Coinbase is an interesting listen.) Here again, I hope and expect that Khurram can attract top-tier in-house talent to share their stories on Khurran’s Quorum.
My thanks to Khurram for the insights and cooperation, and I wish him continued success with his podcast and recruiting agency. On both fronts, he is providing real help to our industry, all informed by his thoughtful and forward-looking approach. It will be exciting to see how his businesses continue to develop over time. I am always open to conducting interviews of this type with other IP thought leaders, so feel free to reach out if you have a compelling perspective to offer.
Please feel free to send comments or questions to me at gaston@k2k.law or via Twitter: @gkroub. Any topic suggestions or thoughts are most welcome.
Gaston Kroub lives in Brooklyn and is a founding partner of K2K IP Law, an intellectual property litigation boutique that also serves as a leading consultancy on patent issues for the investment community. Gaston’s practice focuses on intellectual property litigation and related counseling, with a strong focus on patent matters. You can reach him at gaston@k2k.law or follow him on Twitter: @gkroub.

articles.title: 5 Habits That Keep Great Legal Rainmakers On Top Of Their Game
articles.content:
I’ve been watching tennis for more than 45 years, from Jimmy Connors to Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal, and I still find myself watching Carlos Alcaraz and wondering how he got to a ball I was sure was past him. Then he’ll hit a drop shot from the baseline so soft it barely gets over the net, and I’ll wonder how he even thought to try it. I’ll leave the greatest-of-all-time debate to somebody else, but this guy still shows me things I don’t remember seeing anyone else do.
There’s no arguing with his natural talent, but what fascinates me is what it takes to get to that level and keep finding ways to get better when everyone else is trying to catch you. I see a version of that in the lawyers I work with. After helping hundreds of attorneys build their books of business, I can tell you that the ones who stay at the top don’t all have the same personality. Some would happily work a room of 200 people, while others would rather spend an hour with one person they genuinely want to know. What they do have in common are five habits that keep working long after their first big year.
1. Make Business Development A Non-negotiable
Most lawyers I know say business development is important, but would you know it from looking at their calendars? If the call to a referral partner is the first thing you bump when a client matter heats up, and you never reschedule it, you’ve already decided where business development ranks. The best rainmakers take their commitments to future clients as seriously as they take the work they’re doing for current ones. An urgent matter may force you to move a meeting, but that doesn’t mean it has to disappear from your week.
2. Give People A Useful Reason To Remember You
When I talk to lawyers about personal branding, some immediately picture the person on LinkedIn who can turn a trip to the grocery store into an announcement about how great they are. That’s not what I’m suggesting. Think about a question you’ve answered for three clients in the past month and how many other people in their position might be wrestling with it. Write an article, record a short video or talk about it on a podcast, then share it on LinkedIn in language your clients actually use. If a reader forwards it to a colleague because it answers a question they’ve been kicking around, you’ve done more for your reputation than another post telling people how good you are.
3. Go After The Low-Hanging Fruit First
Before you sign up for another networking event, ask yourself when you last checked in with your best client without a bill or an active matter to discuss. The rainmakers I know make time for those conversations and for the strategic partners who already understand what they do and trust them with referrals. And when they want to meet new referral partners, they’ll look for a chance to speak at a conference those people already attend. That gives the right people a reason to come find them afterward and start a much better conversation than “So, what do you do?”
4. Track The Activity That Gets You To The Number
Making business development a priority gets it on your calendar, but tracking what you do tells you whether the time is paying off. If your goal is $3 million in originations and you’re at $2.5 million, the gap alone doesn’t tell you what to do on Monday. Looking at the proposals that need follow-up, the client conversations you’ve been putting off and the referrals that haven’t gone anywhere yet gives you a place to start. The most consistent rainmakers review those activities every week and check their progress against monthly and quarterly goals, when there’s still time to do something about it.
5. Put Your Ego Aside And Stay A Student Of The Game
One of my favorite expressions is that you can’t read the label from inside the bottle. I see this in my peer advisory roundtables when lawyers with terrific books of business bring in pitches they lost and ask the room what they missed. That takes humility when everyone in the room knows how successful you are. Whether you learn from a partner down the hall, a coach, a book, or a podcast, stay curious enough to test what you’re learning. That includes figuring out where AI can save you time and where a conversation with a real person is still the best use of it.
Alcaraz makes that drop shot look like something he just thought of, but I doubt he’d try it under pressure if he hadn’t worked on it when nobody was watching. If you want your next year to be better than your best year, pick the habit you’re most inclined to skip and give it a place on this week’s calendar.
Grow Your Book, Own Your Future, Be That Lawyer.
Steve Fretzin is a five-time bestselling author, host of the BE THAT LAWYER and Future Rainmakers podcasts, and a business development coach who works exclusively with attorneys. For more than 18 years, he has helped lawyers build strong books of business without selling, pitching, or chasing, using his proven Sales-Free Selling™ approach. His clients consistently become top rainmakers and credit his coaching and systems for driving meaningful, measurable growth. Steve can be reached directly at steve@fretzin.com, or through his website at bethatlawyer.com. Connect with him on LinkedIn at https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevefretzin. His ALL NEW BE THAT LAWYER Community is changing how lawyers develop the skills never taught in law school. Learn more at bethatlawyer.com/community.

articles.title: Biglaw Wants ‘Trophy Office Space,’ And Weil Is Leaving A Lot Of It Behind
articles.content:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.
Because law firms in general tend to want that premium space, it means they are really competing with one another for it. [If a firm knows that it will need a large chunk of space, they may need to] get in the market earlier than perhaps they would have before in order to get the space that they need.
— Devon Munos, senior vice president and head of Americas research at Savills, in comments given to Reuters, on why law firms are competing for a limited supply of premium office space. That competition comes as Weil’s dissolution is set to “return more than 400,000 sf of trophy office space to Manhattan, the market’s largest available block,” according to a new Savills report, along with more than 70,000 square feet in Washington, D.C. There’s a “growing split” between high-quality, well-located buildings with amenities and older, less desirable offices, Munos said. With law firm leasing at its strongest third-quarter level since 2018, firms expecting to need a large amount of space may have to start their search earlier to get what they want.
Staci Zaretsky is the managing editor of Above the Law, where she’s worked since 2011. She’d love to hear from you, so please feel free to email her with any tips, questions, comments, or critiques. You can follow her on Bluesky, X/Twitter, and Threads, or connect with her on LinkedIn.
